summary:
Pakistan's Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act 2018 recognises self-perceived gender identity and prohibits discrimination in education, employment, healthcare, housing and access to goods and services. Rules issued under the Act in 2020 introduced a neutral 'X' marker for administrative documents, and a 2010 Supreme Court order had directed free medical and educational facilities, microcredit schemes and job quotas for transgender people.

These protections sit under an unresolved constitutional challenge. On 19 May 2023 the Federal Shariat Court, ruling across 12 shariat petitions, held that sections 2(f), 3 and 7 of the Act, covering the definition of gender identity, the right to self-perceived gender identity and inheritance, do not conform with the petitioners' reading of Islamic principles. In its reasoning the court speculated that the Act could facilitate the rape and sexual assault of women by men disguised as transgender women. Amnesty International called the ruling a blow to the rights of an already beleaguered group and had warned the government on 17 May 2023 not to adopt amendments violating human-rights standards. The struck provisions remain in force pending appeals, and the UK Home Office's November 2025 country note records ongoing legal disputes over the Act's status.

Lethal violence against transgender women is documented in Karachi with specific dates. In November 2024 gunmen shot three transgender women at close range near Karachi, the second deadly attack on the community there in a week. On 21 September 2025 police found the bullet-riddled bodies of three transgender women shot dead on a roadside highway at Memon Goth, Karachi. A February 2026 report describes a wave of violence that has left Pakistani transgender people afraid to go out, including a night-time Karachi shooting in which activists Zehrish Khanzadi and Bindiya Rana were fired at through a door with three bullets and narrowly escaped. The most recent documented lethal incident in this record is the September 2025 Karachi highway killings; no later killing is documented here.

Implementation failure, not absence of law, is the central problem identified by Justice Project Pakistan's policy brief: the 2018 Act's protections have not translated into safeguards against torture and ill-treatment in practice, and the brief makes custody and police-safeguard recommendations. A 21 October 2025 analysis in The News describes trans Pakistanis facing rejection by landlords, dismissal at hospitals and suspicion or ridicule at police stations despite the Act and 2020 Rules. Healthcare access is a documented failure point: in 2016, 23-year-old transgender activist Alisha was shot seven times and left to bleed to death at Lady Reading Hospital in Peshawar while staff argued over whether to take her to the men's or women's ward, and men there taunted her friends. Some transgender women use hormones and silicone under unsupervised conditions because sex-change surgery is rarely available in Pakistan.

An active retrograde legislative push is also documented: Senator Mushtaq Ahmad has proposed a government 'gender re-assignment board' that would control transgender people's official gender identity. Consensual same-sex acts remain criminalised under Pakistan Penal Code section 377, carrying two years to life imprisonment, with the definition unclear and, per Human Dignity Trust (December 2024), only men criminalised. The UK Home Office's November 2025 note assesses that LGBT+ people are unlikely to face state persecution, while the US State Department's 2021 Human Rights Report records societal violence and discrimination and notes that transgender persons (khwaja sira) face harassment and violence despite some legal recognition.

Same-sex partnership has no legal recognition. The Constitution does not mention sexual orientation or gender identity; Part II section 37 pledges to protect marriage and the family, and Part IX section 227 requires all laws to be compatible with Islam as defined by a government-appointed Islamic council. Article 496 of the Penal Code punishes dishonestly going through a marriage ceremony knowing one is not lawfully married with up to seven years' imprisonment. A small clerical body in Lahore (Tanzeem Ittehad-i-Ummat) declared transgender marriages legal under Islamic law in June 2016, but the Federal Shariat Court's May 2023 ruling on self-perceived gender remains unresolved on appeal. In 2005 a tribal council in the Khyber region ordered a man who married a fellow tribesman to leave the area or face death.

Open expression carries personal risk. Pakistani media censors LGBTQ-related news stories: the government blocked Queerpk.com in late 2013, and the Pakistani edition of the International New York Times (Express Tribune) left a blank space where a photo accompanying a same-sex marriage story should have appeared. Penal Code provisions reinforce this: Article 292 bans sale, distribution, exhibition, ownership or importation of 'obscene' books, pamphlets or images; Article 294 prohibits 'obscene' public acts, songs, music or poems; Article 153 penalises inducing students to political activity that disturbs public order with up to two years' imprisonment; and Article 141 designates an assembly of five or more persons an 'unlawful assembly' if its common object is to commit any offence. LGBTQ Pakistanis are generally reluctant to be open about their identity for fear of forced marriage, honour killings, humiliation, blackmail or violence, and a person living openly is likely to face treatment from non-state actors such as Islamist and terrorist groups. A 2016 article by a young Pakistani man in the UK-based Gay Star News had his surname omitted for his security.
tangentialFactors:
Estimates cited in September 2025 place Pakistan's transgender citizen population at approximately 500,000, facing social exclusion and abuse. The HIV epidemic, which began in Pakistan in 1987, is a related public-health backdrop: government estimates from 2004 put nearly 3,000 people living with HIV, critics suggest 70,000 to 80,000, and UNAIDS reports possibly up to 210,000; a 2009 survey found male and transgender sex workers at high risk with limited condom access and little public health education.

The gap between statutory rights and lived status is a recurring theme across sources: The Diplomat (July 2025) describes citizens 'legally recognized, socially forsaken', and Justice Project Pakistan identifies implementation failure rather than absence of law as the core problem. Raw incident counts in this record are drawn from media reports without population denominators, so frequency of reporting should not be read as a per-capita risk ranking.

outOfScopeNotes:
The final appellate outcome of the Federal Shariat Court's 19 May 2023 ruling on sections 2(f), 3 and 7 of the 2018 Act is unresolved in this record; the struck provisions are reported as remaining in force pending appeals as of the November 2025 UK Home Office note, but no later court decision is sourced here.

Whether Senator Mushtaq Ahmad's proposed 'gender re-assignment board' has advanced beyond proposal is not sourced. The record contains no per-capita or population-denominated violence rate for transgender Pakistanis against which the Karachi incidents could be benchmarked, so the magnitude of trans-specific risk relative to general homicide cannot be stated. The most recent documented lethal incident in this record is dated 21 September 2025; no later killing is documented here, and absence of a later report is not evidence that such violence has ended.
